desc:
Given a string s made only of the letters a, b, c and d, count the distinct non-empty palindromic strings that can be obtained as a subsequence of s. Two subsequences that spell the same string count once, even if they use different indices.

The count can be huge, so return it modulo 1,000,000,007.

s = "bccb"  ->  6    (b, c, bb, cc, bcb, bccb)
s = "aaa"   ->  3    (a, aa, aaa)
s = "abcd"  ->  4
constraints: s contains only the characters 'a', 'b', 'c' and 'd'
hints: Count palindromes inside intervals: D(i, j) is the number of distinct non-empty palindromic subsequences of s[i..j]. If the end characters differ, use inclusion-exclusion over the two shorter intervals.

If the end characters are equal to c, every palindrome that starts and ends with c has the form c + X + c where X is empty or a palindrome from the inside, plus the single 'c'. Duplicates arise when c also occurs inside, so look at the first and last occurrence of c strictly inside the interval.

Let l and r be the first and last c strictly inside (i, j). None inside: 2 * D(i+1, j-1) + 2. Exactly one (l == r): 2 * D(i+1, j-1) + 1. Two or more: 2 * D(i+1, j-1) - D(l+1, r-1). Precompute previous/next occurrence arrays for O(1) lookup.
editorial: If s[i] != s[j], a palindrome in s[i..j] either avoids the left end or avoids the right end, so by inclusion-exclusion D[i][j] = D[i+1][j] + D[i][j-1] - D[i+1][j-1].

If s[i] == s[j] == c, the distinct palindromes of s[i..j] are the ones that already exist strictly inside, counted by D[i+1][j-1], plus new ones that wrap an inside palindrome in c: one string c X c for every inside palindrome X, and also c and cc (the empty X). That gives 2 * D[i+1][j-1] + 2 candidates, but some of them may already be present inside. Let l and r be the first and last occurrences of c strictly between i and j. If there is none, nothing is double counted: 2 * D[i+1][j-1] + 2. If there is exactly one, the string c is already inside: 2 * D[i+1][j-1] + 1. If there are two or more, both c and cc are already inside, and a string c X c is already inside exactly when X can be found between l and r, so subtract D[l+1][r-1] and drop the +2: 2 * D[i+1][j-1] - D[l+1][r-1].

Precompute for every index the next and previous index holding the same letter so each cell costs O(1). Total time is O(n²) with an n × n table (about a million cells), taking all values modulo 10<sup>9</sup>+7. Enumerating subsequences and inserting them into a set is exponential.
